'''Jeremy Mark Berg''' (born April 10, 1958) is a well-known scientific researcher, administrator, communicator, and science advocate. He is currently Professor of Computational and Systems Biology at the University of Pittsburgh School of Medicine. He had previous served as Director of the Department of Biophysics and Biophysical Chemistry at Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine, Director of the National Institute of General Medical Sciences (NIGMS) at the National Institutes of Health (NIH), and Editor-in-Chief of ''Science'' magazine and the ''Science'' family of journals.

== Education ==
Berg earned his bachelor's and master's degrees from [[Stanford University]], where he did research with Keith Hodgson and [[Lubert Stryer]]. He attained his Ph.D. under [[Richard H. Holm]] at [[Harvard University]]. He then completed a post-doctoral fellowship with [[Carl Pabo]] in biophysics at the [[Johns Hopkins School of Medicine]].

== Career ==
Berg started his academic career in the Department of Chemistry at Johns Hopkins University in 1986. He worked on zinc finger proteins, nucleic acid binding proteins that require bound zinc ions for their structures and nucleic acid-binding properties. There, he successfully predicted the three-dimensional structure of TFIIIA-type zinc finger domains prior to the experimental determination of their structures<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Berg |first=J M |date=January 1988 |title=Proposed structure for the zinc-binding domains from transcription factor IIIA and related proteins. |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences |language=en |volume=85 |issue=1 |pages=99–102 |doi=10.1073/pnas.85.1.99 |doi-access=free |issn=0027-8424 |pmc=279490 |pmid=3124104 |bibcode=1988PNAS...85...99B }}</ref><sup>,</sup>.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Lee |first1=Min S. |last2=Gippert |first2=Garry P. |last3=Soman |first3=Kizhake V. |last4=Case |first4=David A. |last5=Wright |first5=Peter E. |date=1989-08-11 |title=Three-Dimensional Solution Structure of a Single Zinc Finger DNA-Binding Domain |url=https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.2503871 |journal=Science |publisher=American Association for the Advancement of Science |volume=245 |issue=4918 |pages=635–637 |doi=10.1126/science.2503871 |pmid=2503871 |bibcode=1989Sci...245..635L |url-access=subscription }}</ref> In 1990, he moved to become Director of the Department of Biophysics and Biophysical Chemistry at Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine at the age of 32, making him the youngest department director at Johns Hopkins since its founding four physicians.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Smith |first1=R. J. |last2=Bryant |first2=R. G. |date=1975-10-27 |title=Metal substitutions incarbonic anhydrase: a halide ion probe study |journal=Biochemical and Biophysical Research Communications |volume=66 |issue=4 |pages=1281–1286 |doi=10.1016/0006-291x(75)90498-2 |issn=0006-291X |pmid=3 |bibcode=1975BBRC...66.1281S }}</ref> In 2003, he moved to NIH to become the Director of NIGMS<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Smith |first1=R. J. |last2=Bryant |first2=R. G. |date=1975-10-27 |title=Metal substitutions incarbonic anhydrase: a halide ion probe study |journal=Biochemical and Biophysical Research Communications |volume=66 |issue=4 |pages=1281–1286 |doi=10.1016/0006-291x(75)90498-2 |issn=0006-291X |pmid=3 |bibcode=1975BBRC...66.1281S }}</ref> where he served until 2011. He then moved to the University of Pittsburgh School of Medicine, following his wife, leading breast imaging researcher Wendie A. Berg, MD, PhD where he became Professor of Computational and Systems Biology and Associate Senior Vice Chancellor for Science Strategy and Planning in the Health Sciences.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Hendrickson |first1=W. A. |last2=Ward |first2=K. B. |date=1975-10-27 |title=Atomic models for the polypeptide backbones of myohemerythrin and hemerythrin |journal=Biochemical and Biophysical Research Communications |volume=66 |issue=4 |pages=1349–1356 |doi=10.1016/0006-291x(75)90508-2 |issn=1090-2104 |pmid=5 |bibcode=1975BBRC...66.1349H }}</ref> In 2013, he became founding director of the University of Pittsburgh/UPMC Institute of Personalized (now Precision) Medicine.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Chow |first1=Y. W. |last2=Pietranico |first2=R. |last3=Mukerji |first3=A. |date=1975-10-27 |title=Studies of oxygen binding energy to hemoglobin molecule |journal=Biochemical and Biophysical Research Communications |volume=66 |issue=4 |pages=1424–1431 |doi=10.1016/0006-291x(75)90518-5 |issn=0006-291X |pmid=6 |bibcode=1975BBRC...66.1424C }}</ref> He took a leave of absence from 2016-2019 to serve as Editor-in-Chief of ''Science'' magazine and the ''Science'' family of journals.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Anderson |first1=T. Effects of morphine |journal=Biochemical Pharmacology |volume=24 |issue=16 |pages=1469–1474 |doi=10.1016/0006-2952(75)90020-9 |issn=1873-2968 |pmid=7}}</ref> 

Berg is the co-author of several leading textbooks including the textbook [[Biochemistry (Stryer)|''Biochemistry'']], originally written by Lubert Stryer.<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Berg |first1=Jeremy M. |title=Biochemistry: tenth edition |last2=Tymoczko |first2=John L. |last3=Gatto |first3=Gregory J. |last4=Stryer |first4=Lubert |last5=Hines |first5=Justin |last6=Heller |first6=Jutta Beneken |date=2023 |publisher=macmillan learning |isbn=978-1-319-33362-1 |edition=Tenth |location=Austin Boston New York Plymouth}}</ref> ''Biochemistry'' is currently in its tenth edition and is widely used by many universities around the world. Previous, he wrote ''Principles of Bioinorganic Chemistry'' with [[Stephen J. Lippard]].<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Lippard |first1=Stephen J. |title=Principles of bioinorganic chemistry |last2=Berg |first2=Jeremy M. |date=1994 |publisher=University Science Books |isbn=978-0-935702-72-9 |location=Mill Valley, Calif}}</ref>

==Awards and honors==
His honors include a Presidential Young Investigator Award (1988–1993), the American Chemical Society Award in Pure Chemistry (1993),<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.acs.org/funding/awards/acs-award-in-pure-chemistry/recipients.html |access-date=2026-09-21 |website=www.acs.org|title=ACS Award in Pure Chemistry Recipients}}</ref> the Eli Lilly Award for Fundamental Research in Biological Chemistry (1995),<ref>{{Cite news |date=January 23, 1995 |title=Jeremy Berg to receive Eli Lilly Award |url=https://pubs.acs.org/cenear/article-pdf/73/4/68/12057940/cen-v073n004.p068.pdf |work=C&EN |page=68}}</ref> the Maryland Outstanding Young Scientist of the Year (1995),<ref>{{Cite web |title=Past OYS Recipients |url=https://www.mdsci.org/educational-programs/awards-scholarships/outstanding-young-scientist/past-oys-recipients/ |access-date=2026-09-21 |website=Maryland Science Center |language=en-US}}</ref> the Distinguished Service Award from the Biophysical Society (2009),<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.eurekalert.org/news-releases/554314 |access-date=2026-09-21 |website=www.eurekalert.org|title=Biophysical Society selects 2009 Distinguished Service, Emily M. Gray and Society Fellow recipients}}</ref> the Howard K. Schachman Public Service Award from the American Society for Biochemistry and Molecular Biology (ASBMB) (2011, presented in 2010),<ref>{{Cite web |title=Howard K. Schachman Public Service Award |url=https://www.asbmb.org/advocacy/public-service-award |access-date=2026-09-21 |website=www.asbmb.org |language=en}}</ref> election to the Institute of Medicine of the National Academies (now the National Academy of Medicine) (2010),<ref>{{Cite web |title=The National Academy of Medicine {{!}} NIH Intramural Research Program |url=https://irp.nih.gov/about-us/honors/the-national-academy-of-medicine |access-date=2026-09-21 |website=irp.nih.gov}}</ref> a Public Service Award from the American Chemical Society (2011),<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Erickson |first=Britt |date=November 12, 2010 |title=BERG, NEUREITER RECEIVE ACS HONOR AWARDS: Society bestows 2011 Public Service Award on two chemists |url=https://pubs.acs.org/cenear/article-abstract/89/17/9/956305/BERG-NEUREITER-RECEIVE-ACS-HONORAWARDS-Society?redirectedFrom=fulltext |access-date=September 21, 2026 |website=ACS, Publications |volume=89 |issue=17 |page=9 |doi=10.1021/cen-v089n017.p009 |url-access=subscription }}</ref> election to the American Academy of Arts and Sciences,<ref>{{Cite web |date=2026-08-10 |title=Jeremy M. Berg {{!}} American Academy of Arts and Sciences |url=https://www.amacad.org/person/jeremy-m-berg |access-date=2026-09-21 |website=www.amacad.org |language=en}}</ref> and election as ASBMB president in 2012. He also received teaching awards from both medical students and graduate students and served as an advisor to the Johns Hopkins Postdoctoral Association at the time of its founding.

== Advocacy ==
While at NIGMS, Berg worked to increase transparency about NIH and its processes. He started the first NIH institute director-written blog, the NIGMS Feedback Loop where he shared data about peer review outcomes and funding probabilities, internal processes for program development, program evaluations, and other aspects of NIGMS operations.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Jeremy Berg {{!}} National Institute of General Medical Sciences |url=https://nigms.nih.gov/loop/author/dr-jeremy-berg |access-date=2026-09-21 |website=nigms.nih.gov}}</ref> At NIH, he developed a strong reputation for taking principled stands.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Kaiser |first=Jocelyn |date=2011-04-29 |title=Jeremy Berg: An Independent Scientist Departs NIH's Ranks |url=https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.332.6029.533 |journal=Science |language=en |volume=332 |issue=6029 |pages=533 |doi=10.1126/science.332.6029.533 |pmid=21527691 |issn=0036-8075|url-access=subscription }}</ref> NIGMS. After his departure from NIGMS, he continued these efforts as elected president of the American Society of Biochemistry and Molecular Biology in 2012. With the beginning of the second administration of Donald J. Trump, he shared information and insights about NIH operations through his Bluesky account (@jeremymberg.bsky.social) and other communication channels.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Jeremy Berg is helping keep researchers nationwide up to date |url=https://www.utimes.pitt.edu/news/jeremy-berg-helping-keep |access-date=2026-09-21 |website=utimes |language=en}}</ref> He worked with current and former NIH staff members to publicize the Bethesda Declaration, a letter of dissent sent to NIH Director Jayanta Bhattacaharya.<ref>{{Citation |title=Bethesda Declaration |date=2026-09-07 |work=Wikipedia |url=https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bethesda_Declaration&oldid=1373746894 |access-date=2026-09-21 |language=en}}</ref> He tracked commitment of NIH funds across fiscal year 2025 when NIH was committing their appropriated funds are rates substantially lower than historical norms. The funding curves that Berg created are now updated regularly on the website grant-witness.org<ref>{{Cite web |last=Witness |first=Grant |title=Agency Pulse: Grantmaking at NIH |url=https://grantwitness.org/nih/analyses/agency-pulse-nih-grantmaking |access-date=2026-09-21 |website=Grant Witness |language=en-US}}</ref> and on the front page of the NIH Reporter website.<ref>{{Cite web |title=RePORT ⟩ RePORTER |url=https://reporter.nih.gov/ |access-date=2026-09-21 |website=reporter.nih.gov}}</ref> He wrote emails to NIH Director Bhattacharya, initially to alert him to historical NIH accomplishments and behavior and to share analyses on ongoing NIH activities. Berg shared these emails on Bluesky and put them together in a compilation called ''50 Shades of Jay''.<ref>{{Cite book |last=M. Berg |first=Jeremy |title=Fifty Shades of 'Jay' |date=2025 |language=English|url=https://jeremymberg.github.io/jeremyberg.github.io/Fifty%20Shades%20of%20Jay-Rev-5-27-26.pdf}}</ref> Berg provide declarations in several lawsuits about historically abnormal NIH terminations of grants. Berg served on the advisory board of the advocacy organization Stand Up for Science.<ref>{{Cite web |title=STAND UP FOR SCIENCE |url=https://www.standupforscience.net/ |access-date=2026-09-21 |website=STAND UP FOR SCIENCE |language=en-US}}</ref>
